whyItExists.problem: HTML defines the structure of a page, but it is static. To update the page dynamically — change text, hide elements, show a popup — JavaScript needs a way to read and modify the HTML document.
whyItExists.solution: The DOM (Document Object Model) is the browser's live representation of the HTML page as a tree of objects. JavaScript can traverse and modify this tree to update the page without reloading.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Any time you need to read or change the page dynamically — update text, toggle a class, show/hide elements, read form values.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: In frameworks like React or Vue, you rarely touch the DOM directly — the framework handles it. But understanding the DOM is essential to understand what the framework is doing for you.

explainModes.beginner: The DOM is JavaScript's view of your HTML page. document.querySelector('#title') finds the element with id='title'. element.textContent = 'Hello' changes its text. element.classList.add('active') adds a CSS class.
explainModes.simple: document.querySelector(selector) returns the first matching element (like CSS selectors). document.querySelectorAll returns a NodeList of all matches. Once you have an element, use textContent, innerHTML, style, classList, and getAttribute to read and change it.
explainModes.standard: querySelector and querySelectorAll accept any valid CSS selector. getElementById, getElementsByClassName are older alternatives but still fast. The element object has properties: textContent (text only), innerHTML (HTML markup), style (inline CSS), classList (class manipulation), value (for inputs), dataset (data-* attributes).
explainModes.technical: The DOM is a tree of Node objects. Element extends Node. Accessing the DOM causes layout/reflow — minimize reads and writes, batch DOM changes, or use a DocumentFragment. innerHTML is vulnerable to XSS — always use textContent for user-provided data or sanitize HTML before injecting.
explainModes.deepDive: The DOM is defined by the WHATWG DOM Living Standard. Every element is an EventTarget, Node, and Element (in that prototype order). Layout recalculation (reflow) is triggered by reading layout properties (offsetWidth, getBoundingClientRect) after DOM mutations — this is called layout thrashing. The Intersection Observer API observes visibility without polling. Virtual DOM frameworks (React) batch mutations into a single flush to minimize reflows.

questions.question: What does document.querySelector('.card') return?
options: An array of all matching elements
questions.explanation: querySelector returns the FIRST matching element. To get all matches, use querySelectorAll, which returns a NodeList.

questions.question: Why should you use textContent instead of innerHTML for user data?
options: textContent prevents XSS — it treats the value as plain text, not HTML
questions.explanation: innerHTML parses the string as HTML, so malicious input like <script>alert('hack')</script> would execute. textContent treats it as literal text and renders it safely.

faq.q: What is the difference between querySelector and getElementById?
faq.a: getElementById is slightly faster and only works with IDs. querySelector accepts any CSS selector (#id, .class, element, [attr]). In modern code, querySelector is preferred for consistency.

faq.q: What is the difference between textContent and innerText?
faq.a: textContent returns all text, including hidden elements and script content. innerText returns only visible text and is affected by CSS (display:none elements are excluded). textContent is faster and generally preferred.
